questions.prompt: In the three-way handshake, what does the server's SYN-ACK acknowledge?
options: The first byte of application data
questions.explanation: The SYN consumes one sequence number, so the server ACKs client ISN + 1 while also announcing its own ISN.

questions.prompt: Which window protects the receiver from being overwhelmed?
questions.explanation: Flow control uses the receiver-advertised rwnd; cwnd is congestion control, which protects the network.
Three duplicate ACKs signal a likely lost segment, so it is resent before the RTO expires.

questions.prompt: Why does TCP need a three-way handshake instead of two messages?
questions.reference_answer: Each side has to announce its own initial sequence number and get confirmation that the other side received it, which takes SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK. This proves both directions work, and together with random ISNs it prevents old duplicate segments from a previous connection being accepted as a new connection.
key_points: Both sides exchange/synchronize initial sequence numbers
Each side's ISN must be acknowledged, confirming both directions work
Prevents old/delayed duplicate segments from creating or corrupting a new connection

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between flow control and congestion control in TCP.
questions.reference_answer: Flow control protects the receiver: the receiver advertises a receive window (rwnd) limiting unacknowledged data in flight. Congestion control protects the network: the sender maintains a congestion window (cwnd) that grows with slow start/congestion avoidance and shrinks on loss. The sender uses min(rwnd, cwnd).
key_points: Flow control protects the receiver, via the advertised receive window (rwnd)
Congestion control protects the network, via the sender's congestion window (cwnd)
cwnd grows (slow start / congestion avoidance) and shrinks on loss
Effective sending window is min(rwnd, cwnd)
